title: Data Structures & Algorithms
tagline: From arrays to DP. Learn it visually, then prove it with practice.
audience: Working engineers and final-year students preparing for product-company interviews
prerequisites: Comfortable writing loops and functions in one of C++, Python, JavaScript or Go
outcomes: Pick the right data structure for a problem and defend its cost
State the invariant behind an algorithm and use it to avoid off-by-one bugs
Recognise the classic interview patterns and code them cleanly under time pressure

glossary.invariant: a statement true before and after every loop iteration
glossary.load factor: α = n / m, entries stored divided by slots (buckets) available

chapters.title: Binary Search
chapters.summary: One comparison against a sorted midpoint discards half the candidates.
outcomes: State the invariant and use it to avoid off-by-one bugs

figures.object: rack of sorted gauge blocks with two sliding stops and a drop probe

chapters.title: Hashing
chapters.summary: A hash function turns a key into a slot number, so lookup is one jump, until collisions pile up.
outcomes: Explain why a hash map lookup is O(1) on average and what the average assumes
Implement separate chaining and linear probing, including deletion with tombstones
Use the load factor to decide when to resize, and show why doubling is amortised O(1)
Recognise the inputs that make a hash map O(n) and what languages do about it

figures.concept: the dial turns a key straight into a tray number; colliding keys stack in one tray, and patterned keys stack in one tray only
figures.object: gantry tray sorter: hash dial, shuttle on an overhead rail, eight trays where colliding keys stack

chapters.title: Stacks, queues & monotonic stacks
chapters.summary: Only one end is reachable, and that restriction is what makes them fast and useful.
outcomes: Use a monotonic stack to answer next-greater queries in O(n)

figures.concept: only the top plate is reachable
